Uses, 12 mo | 1,284 · Related PRB0040012, INC0010023

## Symptom.

The user can reach the internet but the VPN client reports an authentication failure. It began after a password reset. The client may report “invalid credentials” even when the new password is entered correctly.

## Cause.

The VPN client caches the previous credential in the operating system credential store. The cached entry is presented before the newly typed password, so the directory rejects it. Repeated attempts can lock the account (see KB0005).

## Resolution.

1. Confirm with the user that they changed their password within the last 24 hours.

2. Ask the user to sign out of the VPN client completely, including the system tray icon.

3. Clear the cached credential for the VPN profile from the credential store.

4. Reconnect using the new password.

5. If authentication still fails, check whether the account is locked in the identity console before escalating.

## Escalation.

If the account is not locked and the new password works elsewhere, escalate to the Network team with the client log.

## Symptom.

The connection drops every few minutes and reconnects on its own. It is worse in some parts of the building and while moving between areas.

## Cause.

Aggressive roaming behaviour between access points, or a power-saving setting on the wireless adapter that suspends the radio during idle periods.

## Resolution.

1. Establish whether drops occur in one location or while moving. Drops only while moving indicate roaming; drops while stationary indicate the adapter.

2. For a stationary user, disable power saving on the wireless adapter.

3. Update the wireless adapter driver to the current supported version.

4. Ask the user to forget and rejoin the corporate network so the profile is rebuilt.

5. Confirm a stable connection for at least fifteen minutes before closing.

## Escalation.

Drops affecting several users in the same area are an infrastructure fault. Escalate to Network with the location and the approximate times.

## Symptom.

Documents accumulate in the print queue. The printer shows ready and reports no error. Cancelling a job leaves it stuck as Deleting.

## Cause.

The local print spooler service has stalled, leaving orphaned job files that block the queue.

## Resolution.

1. Confirm the printer is online and shows no physical error, and that paper and toner are present.

2. Stop the print spooler service on the affected machine.

3. Delete the queued job files from the spooler directory.

4. Start the print spooler service again.

5. Print a test page and confirm it completes.

## Escalation.

If the queue stalls again within an hour, or several users on the same printer are affected, escalate to Print Services – the fault is likely on the print server rather than the client.

## Symptom.

The machine is noticeably slower after an update. Fans run constantly, applications are slow to launch, and the problem persists across restarts.

## Cause.

Post-update indexing and driver reinstallation run at high priority for a period after installation. If the degradation persists beyond that period, a driver mismatch is the usual cause.

## Resolution.

1. Ask when the update was installed. Within 24 hours, background indexing is expected – tell the user and check back rather than making changes.

2. Check resource usage and identify the dominant process.

3. If indexing dominates, allow it to complete and confirm with the user the following day.

4. If a graphics or storage driver dominates, reinstall the vendor driver for the installed operating system build.

5. Restart and confirm the machine returns to normal responsiveness

nfirm the machine returns to normal responsiveness.

## Escalation.

If performance is still degraded 48 hours after the update with no dominant process, escalate to Endpoint Engineering with a performance capture.
cases.diagnosis:
The root cause is a mechanical failure of the printer's paper feed roller.
Evidence record 7.3 (INC0010047) describes an identical scenario involving a grinding noise during paper feed while the queue was empty. The record explicitly confirms that this symptom indicates a physical mechanical fault rather than a print queue stall (ruling out KB0004). Facilities diagnosed the fault directly to the paper feed roller.
cases.resolution:
Based on the human comments: The incident was determined to be a physical mechanical fault causing a grinding noise rather than a print queue issue, requiring the device to be taken out of service and referred to Facilities for hardware repair, the solution of this incident is:

1. Inspect the printer to confirm whether the issue is a mechanical hardware fault (such as a grinding noise during paper feed) rather than a software queue error. [Source: 7.3]
2. Mark the device and room as out of use for printing until the physical inspection and repairs are completed. [Source: 7.3]
3. Reassign and refer the ticket to the Facilities duty manager for physical hardware intervention. [Source: 7.3]
4. Replace the mechanical paper feed roller and conduct a test print to confirm normal printing functionality with the user. [Source: 7.3]

cases.query: Order service returning 500s under load, pool saturation on dashboard
evidence:
## The trigger.

At 12:58 the order service began returning HTTP 500 under normal midday load. Connection pool saturation was reported in the application log within a minute, and monitoring raised INC0009884 at 13:02 as a P1.

## The response.

The analyst on the bridge searched the knowledge base, found KB0010, and applied it. Step 1 of that article, as it stood, instructed a restart of the application server.

## The consequence.

The restart cleared the pool as documented and simultaneously dropped every in-flight order. The service returned 200 within ninety seconds, so the restart looked successful on every signal the bridge was watching.

## The discovery.

Fulfilment noticed missing orders at 13:31. The bridge was reconvened, the gap was quantified at 47 unrecoverable orders, and manual recovery began.

## Restoration.

The service itself was never unavailable after 13:04. The forty minutes recorded above is the window in which orders were being accepted and lost, which is the number that matters commercially and the one this report uses.

The article was not wrong when it was written.

KB0010 v1 was published in 2023 against an earlier deployment where the service drained gracefully on shutdown. That behaviour changed with the 2025 platform migration and the article was never revisited.

State | Published

Owner | Platform Engineering · K. Selim

Reviewed | 02 Apr 2026

Related | MIR-2026-03, PRB0040018, CHG0030455, INC0010052

## Symptom.

The order service returns HTTP 500 under load. Application logs report that the database connection pool is exhausted and that connection acquisition timed out.

## Cause.

Connections are held beyond their intended lifetime by a long-running query path and are not returned to the pool, so new requests wait and then fail.

## Resolution.

1. Do not restart the application server. A restart drops in-flight orders and caused a 40-minute outage on 14 March 2026.

2. Confirm pool saturation from the service metrics dashboard rather than from the error message alone.

3. Notify the Order Processing service owner. This service has a change-controlled remediation path.

4. Raise an emergency change against CHG0030455 for the pool drain procedure, which recycles connections without dropping in-flight work.

s without dropping in-flight work.

5. Apply the drain procedure only once the change is approved.

6. Monitor pool utilisation for thirty minutes after the drain.

## Escalation.

Any incident on order-processing at Priority 1 goes to the service owner immediately and is never remediated from the service desk alone.

evidence:
State | Published

Version | 3

Service | corporate-email

Category | software

Owner | Collaboration Services

Author | O. Sabry

Reviewed | 02 Feb 2026

Uses, 12 mo | 947 · Related INC0010024

## Symptom.

The mail client displays Disconnected or Trying to connect. No new mail arrives. Webmail may still work, or may not.

## Cause.

Two distinct causes present identically: a single-user profile or cached-mode corruption, and a service-wide mail outage. Distinguishing them is the first step, not an afterthought.

## Resolution.

1. Ask whether colleagues are affected. If more than one user in the same area is affected, treat it as a service event and stop; do not apply per-user fixes to a platform outage.

2. Check whether webmail works for this user. If webmail works, the fault is client-side.

3. For a client-side fault, close the client fully and reopen it.

4. If it still fails, recreate the mail profile and allow the cache to rebuild.

5. Confirm mail flow before closing.

## Escalation.

If multiple users are affected, raise a major incident against the corporate-email service. Do not resolve individual incidents until the service event is closed.

Reviewed | 06 Oct 2025

## Symptom.

The SAP GUI client fails to connect and reports RFC_ERROR_COMMUNICATION or a connection timeout. Other applications work normally.

3. If the entry names a specific application server, change it to the message server and group so that load balancing applies.

4. Reconnect and confirm sign-in reaches the logon screen.

5. If the timeout persists from a known-good network, check whether the message server is reach

network, check whether the message server is reachable on its port before escalating.

## Escalation.

A confirmed reachability failure from the corporate network goes to the SAP Basis team with the exact error text and the connection entry used.

s without dropping in-flight work.

5. Apply the drain procedure only once the change is approved.

6. Monitor pool utilisation for thirty minutes after the drain.

## Symptom.

The user can reach the internet but the VPN client reports an authentication failure. It began after a password reset. The client may report “invalid credentials” even when the new password is entered correctly.

## Cause.

The VPN client caches the previous credential in the operating system credential store. The cached entry is presented before the newly typed password, so the directory rejects it. Repeated attempts can lock the account (see KB0005).

## Resolution.

1. Confirm with the user that they changed their password within the last 24 hours.

2. Ask the user to sign out of the VPN client completely, including the system tray icon.

3. Clear the cached credential for the VPN profile from the credential store.

4. Reconnect using the new password.

5. If authentication still fails, check whether the account is locked in the identity console before escalating.

## Escalation.

If the account is not locked and the new password works elsewhere, escalate to the Network team with the client log.

## Symptom.

The mail client displays Disconnected or Trying to connect. No new mail arrives. Webmail may still work, or may not.

## Cause.

Two distinct causes present identically: a single-user profile or cached-mode corruption, and a service-wide mail outage. Distinguishing them is the first step, not an afterthought.

## Resolution.

1. Ask whether colleagues are affected. If more than one user in the same area is affected, treat it as a service event and stop; do not apply per-user fixes to a platform outage.

2. Check whether webmail works for this user. If webmail works, the fault is client-side.

3. For a client-side fault, close the client fully and reopen it.

4. If it still fails, recreate the mail profile and allow the cache to rebuild.

5. Confirm mail flow before closing.

## Escalation.

If multiple users are affected, raise a major incident against the corporate-email service. Do not resolve individual incidents until the service event is closed.

ORDER SERVICE CONNECTION POOL EXHAUSTION

State | Published

Version | 2

Service | order-processing

Owner | Platform Engineering · K. Selim

Reviewed | 02 Apr 2026

Related | MIR-2026-03, PRB0040018, CHG0030455, INC0010052

## Symptom.

The order service returns HTTP 500 under load. Application logs report that the database connection pool is exhausted and that connection acquisition timed out.

## Cause.

Connections are held beyond their intended lifetime by a long-running query path and are not returned to the pool, so new requests wait and then fail.

## Resolution.

1. Do not restart the application server. A restart drops in-flight orders and caused a 40-minute outage on 14 March 2026.

2. Confirm pool saturation from the service metrics dashboard rather than from the error message alone.

3. Notify the Order Processing service owner. This service has a change-controlled remediation path.

4. Raise an emergency change against CHG0030455 for the pool drain procedure, which recycles connections without dropping in-flight work.

5. Apply the d

s without dropping in-flight work.

5. Apply the drain procedure only once the change is approved.

6. Monitor pool utilisation for thirty minutes after the drain.

## Escalation.

Any incident on order-processing at Priority 1 goes to the service owner immediately and is never remediated from the service desk alone.

## The trigger.

At 12:58 the order service began returning HTTP 500 under normal midday load. Connection pool saturation was reported in the application log within a minute, and monitoring raised INC0009884 at 13:02 as a P1.

## The response.

The analyst on the bridge searched the knowledge base, found KB0010, and applied it. Step 1 of that article, as it stood, instructed a restart of the application server.

## The consequence.

The restart cleared the pool as documented and simultaneously dropped every in-flight order. The service returned 200 within ninety seconds, so the restart looked successful on every signal the bridge was watching.

## The discovery.

Fulfilment noticed missing orders at 13:31. The bridge was reconvened, the gap was quantified at 47 unrecoverable orders, and manual recovery began.

## Restoration.

The service itself was never unavailable after 13:04. The forty minutes recorded above is the window in which orders were being accepted and lost, which is the number that matters commercially and the one this report uses.

The article was not wrong when it was written.

KB0010 v1 was published in 2023 against an earlier deployment where the service drained gracefully on shutdown. That behaviour changed with the 2025 platform migration and the article was never revisited.

## Symptom.

The machine is noticeably slower after an update. Fans run constantly, applications are slow to launch, and the problem persists across restarts.

## Cause.

Post-update indexing and driver reinstallation run at high priority for a period after installation. If the degradation persists beyond that period, a driver mismatch is the usual cause.

3. If indexing dominates, allow it to complete and confirm with the user the following day.

s without dropping in-flight work.

5. Apply the drain procedure only once the change is approved.

## The trigger.

At 12:58 the order service began returning HTTP 500 under normal midday load. Connection pool saturation was reported in the application log within a minute, and monitoring raised INC0009884 at 13:02 as a P1.

## The response.

The analyst on the bridge searched the knowledge base, found KB0010, and applied it. Step 1 of that article, as it stood, instructed a restart of the application server.

## The consequence.

The restart cleared the pool as documented and simultaneously dropped every in-flight order. The service returned 200 within ninety seconds, so the restart looked successful on every signal the bridge was watching.

## The discovery.

Fulfilment noticed missing orders at 13:31. The bridge was reconvened, the gap was quantified at 47 unrecoverable orders, and manual recovery began.

## Restoration.

The service itself was never unavailable after 13:04. The forty minutes recorded above is the window in which orders were being accepted and lost, which is the number that matters commercially and the one this report uses.

The article was not wrong when it was written.

KB0010 v1 was published in 2023 against an earlier deployment where the service drained gracefully on shutdown. That behaviour changed with the 2025 platform migration and the article was never revisited.

## Symptom.

The mail client displays Disconnected or Trying to connect. No new mail arrives. Webmail may still work, or may not.

## Cause.

Two distinct causes present identically: a single-user profile or cached-mode corruption, and a service-wide mail outage. Distinguishing them is the first step, not an afterthought.

## Resolution.

1. Ask whether colleagues are affected. If more than one user in the same area is affected, treat it as a service event and stop; do not apply per-user fixes to a platform outage.

2. Check whether webmail works for this user. If webmail works, the fault is client-side.

3. For a client-side fault, close the client fully and reopen it.

4. If it still fails, recreate the mail profile and allow the cache to rebuild.

5. Confirm mail flow before closing.

## Escalation.

If multiple users are affected, raise a major incident against the corporate-email service. Do not resolve individual incidents until the service event is closed.

## Symptom.

The user can reach the internet but the VPN client reports an authentication failure. It began after a password reset. The client may report “invalid credentials” even when the new password is entered correctly.

## Cause.

The VPN client caches the previous credential in the operating system credential store. The cached entry is presented before the newly typed password, so the directory rejects it. Repeated attempts can lock the account (see KB0005).

## Resolution.

1. Confirm with the user that they changed their password within the last 24 hours.

2. Ask the user to sign out of the VPN client completely, including the system tray icon.

3. Clear the cached credential for the VPN profile from the credential store.

4. Reconnect using the new password.

5. If authentication still fails, check whether the account is locked in the identity console before escalating.

## Escalation.

If the account is not locked and the new password works elsewhere, escalate to the Network team with the client log.

## Symptom.

Aggressive roaming behaviour between access points, or a power-saving setting on the wireless adapter that suspends the radio during idle periods.

Drops affecting several users in the same area are an infrastructure fault. Escalate to Network with the location and the approximate times.

## Symptom.

The user cannot sign in to any corporate system. Errors mention a locked or disabled account. Often follows a password change, and often presents as several services failing at once.

## Cause.

The lockout policy triggers after a threshold of failed attempts. A cached credential on any device – a phone mail profile, a VPN client, a mapped drive – can retry an old password silently and lock the account repeatedly, including immediately after each unlock.

## Resolution.

1. Verify the user's identity following the identity verification procedure. This step is mandatory and is never skipped.

2. Unlock the account in the identity console.

3. Ask the user to sign out of the corporate mail profile on their mobile device, which is the most common source of a silent retry.

4. Clear cached credentials on the laptop, including VPN and mapped drives.

5. Ask the user to sign in again and confirm access to two different services.

to two different services.

6. If the account locks again within minutes, a device is still retrying an old credential; identify it from the lockout source before unlocking a third time.

## Symptom.

Documents accumulate in the print queue. The printer shows ready and reports no error. Cancelling a job leaves it stuck as Deleting.

## Cause.

The local print spooler service has stalled, leaving orphaned job files that block the queue.

## Resolution.

1. Confirm the printer is online and shows no physical error, and that paper and toner are present.

2. Stop the print spooler service on the affected machine.

3. Delete the queued job files from the spooler directory.

4. Start the print spooler service again.

5. Print a test page and confirm it completes.

## Escalation.

If the queue stalls again within an hour, or several users on the same printer are affected, escalate to Print Services – the fault is likely on the print server rather than the client.

## Symptom.

The connection drops every few minutes and reconnects on its own. It is worse in some parts of the building and while moving between areas.

## Cause.

Aggressive roaming behaviour between access points, or a power-saving setting on the wireless adapter that suspends the radio during idle periods.

## Resolution.

1. Establish whether drops occur in one location or while moving. Drops only while moving indicate roaming; drops while stationary indicate the adapter.

2. For a stationary user, disable power saving on the wireless adapter.

3. Update the wireless adapter driver to the current supported version.

4. Ask the user to forget and rejoin the corporate network so the profile is rebuilt.

5. Confirm a stable connection for at least fifteen minutes before closing.

## Escalation.

Drops affecting several users in the same area are an infrastructure fault. Escalate to Network with the location and the approximate times.

## Symptom.

## Cause.

Post-update indexing and driver reinstallation run at high priority for a period after installation. If the degradation persists beyond that period, a driver mismatch is the usual cause.

1. Verify the user's identity following the enhanced verification procedure for MFA resets. This is stricter than standard verification and must not be shortened.

2. Confirm whether the previous device is lost or simply replaced. A lost device requires the registration to be revoked, not just re-enrolled.

## Escalation.

An MFA reset is a high-risk identity action. It always requires the approval step, and any suspicion of compromise goes to Security immediately.

## The trigger.

At 12:58 the order service began returning HTTP 500 under normal midday load. Connection pool saturation was reported in the application log within a minute, and monitoring raised INC0009884 at 13:02 as a P1.

## The response.

The analyst on the bridge searched the knowledge base, found KB0010, and applied it. Step 1 of that article, as it stood, instructed a restart of the application server.

## The consequence.

The restart cleared the pool as documented and simultaneously dropped every in-flight order. The service returned 200 within ninety seconds, so the restart looked successful on every signal the bridge was watching.

## The discovery.

Fulfilment noticed missing orders at 13:31. The bridge was reconvened, the gap was quantified at 47 unrecoverable orders, and manual recovery began.

## Restoration.

The service itself was never unavailable after 13:04. The forty minutes recorded above is the window in which orders were being accepted and lost, which is the number that matters commercially and the one this report uses.

The article was not wrong when it was written.

KB0010 v1 was published in 2023 against an earlier deployment where the service drained gracefully on shutdown. That behaviour changed with the 2025 platform migration and the article was never revisited.

The SAP GUI client is using a saved connection profile that explicitly points to a decommissioned application server rather than the active message server.
According to KB0008 and KE0000034, SAP GUI connection issues following migrations occur when saved connection entries retain hardcoded references to decommissioned application servers like APPSRV-OLD-04 instead of connecting through the message server. The client is unable to establish a connection because the legacy server target is no longer active.
cases.resolution:
1. Verify that the user is connected to the corporate network or an active VPN, as SAP GUI cannot be reached directly over the internet. [Source: KB0008]

## Symptom.

The user can reach the internet but the VPN client reports an authentication failure. It began after a password reset. The client may report “invalid credentials” even when the new password is entered correctly.

## Cause.

The VPN client caches the previous credential in the operating system credential store. The cached entry is presented before the newly typed password, so the directory rejects it. Repeated attempts can lock the account (see KB0005).

## Resolution.

1. Confirm with the user that they changed their password within the last 24 hours.

2. Ask the user to sign out of the VPN client completely, including the system tray icon.

3. Clear the cached credential for the VPN profile from the credential store.

4. Reconnect using the new password.

5. If authentication still fails, check whether the account is locked in the identity console before escalating.

## Escalation.

If the account is not locked and the new password works elsewhere, escalate to the Network team with the client log.

## The trigger.

At 12:58 the order service began returning HTTP 500 under normal midday load. Connection pool saturation was reported in the application log within a minute, and monitoring raised INC0009884 at 13:02 as a P1.

## The response.

The analyst on the bridge searched the knowledge base, found KB0010, and applied it. Step 1 of that article, as it stood, instructed a restart of the application server.

## The consequence.

The restart cleared the pool as documented and simultaneously dropped every in-flight order. The service returned 200 within ninety seconds, so the restart looked successful on every signal the bridge was watching.

## The discovery.

Fulfilment noticed missing orders at 13:31. The bridge was reconvened, the gap was quantified at 47 unrecoverable orders, and manual recovery began.

## Restoration.

The service itself was never unavailable after 13:04. The forty minutes recorded above is the window in which orders were being accepted and lost, which is the number that matters commercially and the one this report uses.

The article was not wrong when it was written.

KB0010 v1 was published in 2023 against an earlier deployment where the service drained gracefully on shutdown. That behaviour changed with the 2025 platform migration and the article was never revisited.

## Symptom.

The machine is noticeably slower after an update. Fans run constantly, applications are slow to launch, and the problem persists across restarts.

## Cause.

Post-update indexing and driver reinstallation run at high priority for a period after installation. If the degradation persists beyond that period, a driver mismatch is the usual cause.

## Resolution.

1. Ask when the update was installed. Within 24 hours, background indexing is expected – tell the user and check back rather than making changes.

2. Check resource usage and identify the dominant process.

3. If indexing dominates, allow it to complete and confirm with the user the following day.

4. If a graphics or storage driver dominates, reinstall the vendor driver for the installed operating system build.

5. Restart and confirm the machine returns to normal responsiveness

nfirm the machine returns to normal responsiveness.

## Escalation.

If performance is still degraded 48 hours after the update with no dominant process, escalate to Endpoint Engineering with a performance capture.

## Symptom.

The user can reach the internet but the VPN client reports an authentication failure. It began after a password reset. The client may report “invalid credentials” even when the new password is entered correctly.

## Cause.

The VPN client caches the previous credential in the operating system credential store. The cached entry is presented before the newly typed password, so the directory rejects it. Repeated attempts can lock the account (see KB0005).

## Resolution.

1. Confirm with the user that they changed their password within the last 24 hours.

2. Ask the user to sign out of the VPN client completely, including the system tray icon.

3. Clear the cached credential for the VPN profile from the credential store.

4. Reconnect using the new password.

5. If authentication still fails, check whether the account is locked in the identity console before escalating.

## Escalation.

If the account is not locked and the new password works elsewhere, escalate to the Network team with the client log.

## Symptom.

The SAP GUI client fails to connect and reports RFC_ERROR_COMMUNICATION or a connection timeout. Other applications work normally.

## Cause.

The client cannot reach the message server on the required port. Most often the user is off the corporate network without the VPN, or the saved connection entry points at a decommissioned application server.

## Resolution.

1. Confirm the user is on the corporate network or connected to the VPN. SAP is not reachable from the internet.

2. Check the saved connection entry against the current published connection details.

3. If the entry names a specific application server, change it to the message server and group so that load balancing applies.

4. Reconnect and confirm sign-in reaches the logon screen.

5. If the timeout persists from a known-good network, check whether the message server is reach

network, check whether the message server is reachable on its port before escalating.

A confirmed reachability failure from the corporate network goes to the SAP Basis team with the exact error text and the connection entry used.

KB0001 explicitly identifies that following a password change, the VPN client retains the previous credential in the OS credential store and presents it before the newly entered password, resulting in directory authentication rejection. Incident record 7.2 (INC0010023) confirms this failure pattern, where a VPN authentication failure occurred directly after a user reset their password.

1. Confirm with the user that their account password was reset within the last 24 hours. [Source: KB0001]
2. Have the user completely sign out of the corporate VPN client, ensuring they also exit the application from the system tray icon. [Source: KB0001]
3. Clear the saved cached credential for the corporate VPN profile from the operating system credential store. [Source: KB0001]
4. Instruct the user to launch the VPN client and connect using their newly updated password. [Source: KB0001]

## Symptom.

The user cannot sign in to any corporate system. Errors mention a locked or disabled account. Often follows a password change, and often presents as several services failing at once.

## Cause.

The lockout policy triggers after a threshold of failed attempts. A cached credential on any device – a phone mail profile, a VPN client, a mapped drive – can retry an old password silently and lock the account repeatedly, including immediately after each unlock.

## Resolution.

1. Verify the user's identity following the identity verification procedure. This step is mandatory and is never skipped.

2. Unlock the account in the identity console.

3. Ask the user to sign out of the corporate mail profile on their mobile device, which is the most common source of a silent retry.

4. Clear cached credentials on the laptop, including VPN and mapped drives.

5. Ask the user to sign in again and confirm access to two different services.

6. If the account lock

to two different services.

6. If the account locks again within minutes, a device is still retrying an old credential; identify it from the lockout source before unlocking a third time.

## Escalation.

Repeated lockouts with no identifiable source go to the Identity team. Never disable the lockout policy for an individual user.

## Symptom.

The user can reach the internet but the VPN client reports an authentication failure. It began after a password reset. The client may report “invalid credentials” even when the new password is entered correctly.

## Cause.

The VPN client caches the previous credential in the operating system credential store. The cached entry is presented before the newly typed password, so the directory rejects it. Repeated attempts can lock the account (see KB0005).

## Resolution.

1. Confirm with the user that they changed their password within the last 24 hours.

2. Ask the user to sign out of the VPN client completely, including the system tray icon.

3. Clear the cached credential for the VPN profile from the credential store.

4. Reconnect using the new password.

5. If authentication still fails, check whether the account is locked in the identity console before escalating.

## Escalation.

If the account is not locked and the new password works elsewhere, escalate to the Network team with the client log.

Escalate on the clock, not on frustration. An incident is escalated when the analyst has exhausted the documented knowledge for its category and the next response target is inside the next hour – whichever comes first. Escalating earlier is not a failure; holding a ticket past its target because you nearly have it is.

cases.diagnosis:
An account lockout occurs following a password reset because cached credentials on a device or application automatically retry authentication using the outdated password, exceeding the system lockout threshold.
According to KB0005 and KB0001, performing a password reset while application profiles (such as mobile mail, VPN clients, or mapped drives) store old credentials leads to background authentication retries using the former password. These silent failed attempts trigger the identity system's lockout policy, resulting in locked accounts and access failures across corporate services.
cases.resolution:
1. Verify the user's identity following the mandatory identity verification procedure prior to taking account actions. [Source: KB0005]

2. Unlock the user's account in the identity console. [Source: KB0005]

3. Have the user sign out of the corporate mail profile on their mobile device to stop silent authentication retries. [Source: KB0005]

4. Ask the user to sign out of the corporate VPN client completely, including exiting the system tray icon, and clear the cached VPN profile credentials from the operating system credential store. [Source: KB0001]

5. Have the user sign in with their new password and verify restored access across two different corporate services. [Source: KB0005]

6. If the account locks again within minutes, identify the specific device retrying outdated credentials from the lockout source log before performing an additional unlock. [Source: KB0005]

## Symptom.

The SAP GUI client fails to connect and reports RFC_ERROR_COMMUNICATION or a connection timeout. Other applications work normally.

## Cause.

The client cannot reach the message server on the required port. Most often the user is off the corporate network without the VPN, or the saved connection entry points at a decommissioned application server.

## Resolution.

1. Confirm the user is on the corporate network or connected to the VPN. SAP is not reachable from the internet.

2. Check the saved connection entry against the current published connection details.

3. If the entry names a specific application server, change it to the message server and group so that load balancing applies.

4. Reconnect and confirm sign-in reaches the logon screen.

5. If the timeout persists from a known-good network, check whether the message server is reach

network, check whether the message server is reachable on its port before escalating.

## Escalation.

A confirmed reachability failure from the corporate network goes to the SAP Basis team with the exact error text and the connection entry used.

Uses, 12 mo | 1,041 · Related PRB0040021, INC0010033

## Symptom.

The connection drops every few minutes and reconnects on its own. It is worse in some parts of the building and while moving between areas.

## Cause.

Aggressive roaming behaviour between access points, or a power-saving setting on the wireless adapter that suspends the radio during idle periods.

## Resolution.

1. Establish whether drops occur in one location or while moving. Drops only while moving indicate roaming; drops while stationary indicate the adapter.

2. For a stationary user, disable power saving on the wireless adapter.

3. Update the wireless adapter driver to the current supported version.

4. Ask the user to forget and rejoin the corporate network so the profile is rebuilt.

5. Confirm a stable connection for at least fifteen minutes before closing.

## Escalation.

Drops affecting several users in the same area are an infrastructure fault. Escalate to Network with the location and the approximate times.

## Symptom.

The order service returns HTTP 500 under load. Application logs report that the database connection pool is exhausted and that connection acquisition timed out.

## Cause.

Connections are held beyond their intended lifetime by a long-running query path and are not returned to the pool, so new requests wait and then fail.

## Resolution.

1. Do not restart the application server. A restart drops in-flight orders and caused a 40-minute outage on 14 March 2026.

2. Confirm pool saturation from the service metrics dashboard rather than from the error message alone.

3. Notify the Order Processing service owner. This service has a change-controlled remediation path.

4. Raise an emergency change against CHG0030455 for the pool drain procedure, which recycles connections without dropping in-flight work.

5. Apply the d

s without dropping in-flight work.

5. Apply the drain procedure only once the change is approved.

6. Monitor pool utilisation for thirty minutes after the drain.

## Escalation.

Any incident on order-processing at Priority 1 goes to the service owner immediately and is never remediated from the service desk alone.

The SAP GUI client fails to connect and reports RFC_ERROR_COMMUNICATION or a connection timeout. Other applications work normally.

ORDER SERVICE CONNECTION POOL EXHAUSTION

State | Published

Version | 2

Service | order-processing

Owner | Platform Engineering · K. Selim

Reviewed | 02 Apr 2026

Related | MIR-2026-03, PRB0040018, CHG0030455, INC0010052

## Symptom.

The order service returns HTTP 500 under load. Application logs report that the database connection pool is exhausted and that connection acquisition timed out.

## Cause.

Connections are held beyond their intended lifetime by a long-running query path and are not returned to the pool, so new requests wait and then fail.

## Resolution.

1. Do not restart the application server. A restart drops in-flight orders and caused a 40-minute outage on 14 March 2026.

2. Confirm pool saturation from the service metrics dashboard rather than from the error message alone.

3. Notify the Order Processing service owner. This service has a change-controlled remediation path.

4. Raise an emergency change against CHG0030455 for the pool drain procedure, which recycles connections without dropping in-flight work.

5. Apply the d

s without dropping in-flight work.

5. Apply the drain procedure only once the change is approved.

6. Monitor pool utilisation for thirty minutes after the drain.

## Escalation.

Any incident on order-processing at Priority 1 goes to the service owner immediately and is never remediated from the service desk alone.

## The trigger.

At 12:58 the order service began returning HTTP 500 under normal midday load. Connection pool saturation was reported in the application log within a minute, and monitoring raised INC0009884 at 13:02 as a P1.

## The response.

The analyst on the bridge searched the knowledge base, found KB0010, and applied it. Step 1 of that article, as it stood, instructed a restart of the application server.

## The consequence.

The restart cleared the pool as documented and simultaneously dropped every in-flight order. The service returned 200 within ninety seconds, so the restart looked successful on every signal the bridge was watching.

## The discovery.

Fulfilment noticed missing orders at 13:31. The bridge was reconvened, the gap was quantified at 47 unrecoverable orders, and manual recovery began.

## Restoration.

The service itself was never unavailable after 13:04. The forty minutes recorded above is the window in which orders were being accepted and lost, which is the number that matters commercially and the one this report uses.

The article was not wrong when it was written.

KB0010 v1 was published in 2023 against an earlier deployment where the service drained gracefully on shutdown. That behaviour changed with the 2025 platform migration and the article was never revisited.

Author | O. Sabry

Uses, 12 mo | 947 · Related INC0010024

## Symptom.

The mail client displays Disconnected or Trying to connect. No new mail arrives. Webmail may still work, or may not.

## Cause.

Two distinct causes present identically: a single-user profile or cached-mode corruption, and a service-wide mail outage. Distinguishing them is the first step, not an afterthought.

## Resolution.

1. Ask whether colleagues are affected. If more than one user in the same area is affected, treat it as a service event and stop; do not apply per-user fixes to a platform outage.

2. Check whether webmail works for this user. If webmail works, the fault is client-side.

3. For a client-side fault, close the client fully and reopen it.

4. If it still fails, recreate the mail profile and allow the cache to rebuild.

5. Confirm mail flow before closing.

## Escalation.

If multiple users are affected, raise a major incident against the corporate-email service. Do not resolve individual incidents until the service event is closed.

cases.diagnosis:
The SAP GUI client cannot reach the SAP message server on the required port, typically because the user is disconnected from the corporate network/VPN or is using a connection entry referencing a decommissioned application server.
According to KB0008, the error RFC_ERROR_COMMUNICATION directly results from the SAP GUI client's inability to establish network reachability to the message server on its designated port. Grounded in the evidence, this underlying reachability failure occurs when a user attempts access from outside the corporate network without a VPN or relies on outdated connection settings pointing to an inactive server.
cases.resolution:
1. Confirm that the user is connected to the corporate network or VPN, as the SAP GUI cannot connect directly over the public internet. [Source: KB0008]

2. Check the user's saved SAP GUI connection entry against the current published connection details. [Source: KB0008]

3. If the saved entry specifies a individual application server rather than the message server, update the connection entry to use the message server and logon group so load balancing is applied. [Source: KB0008]

4. Reconnect through the SAP GUI and verify that the sign-in prompt reaches the logon screen successfully. [Source: KB0008]

5. If the timeout persists from a known-good network connection, test and confirm whether the message server is reachable on its required port before initiating an escalation. [Source: KB0008]

6. If a reachability failure from the corporate network is confirmed, escalate the ticket to the SAP Basis team alongside the exact error text and the connection entry details used. [Source: KB0008]

cases.diagnosis:
The root cause of PRB0040012 is account lockouts resulting from cached, outdated credentials stored on mobile mail profiles attempting authentication after password updates.
As documented in problem record PRB0040012 and incident INC0010064, users experience account lockouts after password changes because mobile mail profiles continue retrying sign-ins using cached credentials. Related known error KE0000047 and knowledge article KB0005 document this pattern where mobile devices continuously submit invalid credentials, causing repeated account lockouts.
cases.resolution:
Based on the human comments: simultaneous service disruptions across email, file shares, and collaboration tools were caused by an account lockout triggered by a mobile mail profile repeatedly authenticating with an outdated cached password, which was resolved by updating the mobile credentials, clearing cached endpoint credentials, and unlocking the account, the solution of this incident is:

1. Access the identity console to identify the lockout source and confirm that the account lock is being triggered by cached credentials on a mobile mail profile before attempting an unlock. [Source: KE0000047]
2. Have the user sign out of the corporate mail profile on their mobile device and re-enter their current password to stop automated failed sign-in attempts. [Source: KB0005]
3. Clear all cached credentials on the user's laptop, including saved credentials for the VPN and other connected services. [Source: CHG0030418]
4. Verify the user's identity per standard verification procedure and unlock the account in the identity console. [Source: CHG0030422]
5. Link the incident to problem record PRB0040012 and monitor the account for 15 minutes to ensure authentication stabilizes without recurring lockouts. [Source: PRB0040012]

## Symptom.

The user cannot sign in to any corporate system. Errors mention a locked or disabled account. Often follows a password change, and often presents as several services failing at once.

## Cause.

The lockout policy triggers after a threshold of failed attempts. A cached credential on any device – a phone mail profile, a VPN client, a mapped drive – can retry an old password silently and lock the account repeatedly, including immediately after each unlock.

## Resolution.

1. Verify the user's identity following the identity verification procedure. This step is mandatory and is never skipped.

2. Unlock the account in the identity console.

3. Ask the user to sign out of the corporate mail profile on their mobile device, which is the most common source of a silent retry.

4. Clear cached credentials on the laptop, including VPN and mapped drives.

5. Ask the user to sign in again and confirm access to two different services.

6. If the account lock

to two different services.

6. If the account locks again within minutes, a device is still retrying an old credential; identify it from the lockout source before unlocking a third time.

## Escalation.

Repeated lockouts with no identifiable source go to the Identity team. Never disable the lockout policy for an individual user.

cases.diagnosis:
The account was locked by the lockout policy due to repeated failed sign-in attempts caused by a device silently retrying a cached old credential.
KB0005 explicitly lists INC0010027 as a related incident and defines the root cause for user accounts becoming locked after a password change. Silent background retries using old credentials cached on a device (such as a mobile mail profile, VPN client, or mapped drive) trigger the lockout policy threshold, causing sign-in failures across multiple corporate services.
cases.resolution:
1. Verify the user's identity following the mandatory identity verification procedure. [Source: KB0005]
2. Unlock the account using the identity console. [Source: KB0005]
3. Instruct the user to sign out of the corporate mail profile on their mobile device to stop silent credential retry attempts. [Source: KB0005]
4. Clear cached credentials stored on the laptop, including cached passwords for the VPN client and mapped network drives. [Source: KB0005]
5. Have the user sign in again with their updated credentials and confirm successful access to at least two different services. [Source: KB0005]
6. Monitor the account status, and if it locks again within minutes, determine the retrying device from the lockout source before attempting a third unlock, escalating to the Identity team if the source cannot be identified. [Source: KB0005]

## Symptom.

The user has a new phone, or has lost the previous one, and can no longer approve sign-in prompts or generate codes.

## Cause.

The authenticator registration is bound to the previous device and does not transfer with a phone migration.

## Resolution.

1. Verify the user's identity following the enhanced verification procedure for MFA resets. This is stricter than standard verification and must not be shortened.

2. Confirm whether the previous device is lost or simply replaced. A lost device requires the registration to be revoked, not just re-enrolled.

3. Raise the MFA reset request through the identity workflow. It requires approval; a service desk agent cannot complete it alone.

4. Once approved, guide the user through en

lone.

4. Once approved, guide the user through enrolling the new device.

5. Confirm a successful sign-in with the new factor before closing.

## Escalation.

An MFA reset is a high-risk identity action. It always requires the approval step, and any suspicion of compromise goes to Security immediately.

cases.diagnosis:
The multi-factor authenticator registration remains bound to a previous device and does not transfer automatically following a device replacement or migration.
Record RITM0010877 represents an MFA reset request resulting from a lost or replaced phone. According to KB0006, users are unable to approve sign-in prompts or generate verification codes because authenticator registrations are tied specifically to the user's prior device and fail to transfer with phone migration.
cases.resolution:
1. Verify the user's identity by following the strict enhanced verification procedure required for MFA resets. [Source: KB0006]
2. Confirm whether the user's previous device was lost or replaced; if the device is lost, ensure its MFA registration is revoked rather than simply re-enrolled. [Source: KB0006]
3. Submit an MFA reset request through the identity workflow to obtain the necessary approval, as this action cannot be completed by a service desk agent alone. [Source: KB0006]
4. After approval is secured, guide the user through the process of enrolling their new device. [Source: KB0006]
5. Validate that the user can successfully complete a sign-in using the new authentication factor prior to resolving the ticket. [Source: KB0006]

According to the service context, repeated 5 GHz wireless drops occurring in a specific area while roaming between access points constitute an infrastructure fault rather than individual endpoint failures. Known error documentation KE0000052 and problem record PRB0040021 explicitly identify this roaming issue on floors 3 and 4 as a wireless controller firmware fault.
cases.resolution:
1. Verify that the incident involves 5 GHz corporate Wi-Fi drops on floors 3 and 4, recognizing that multiple reports in this area indicate an infrastructure issue rather than an individual endpoint fault. [Source: KB0009]

3. Inform roaming users that there is no endpoint workaround for drops while moving between floors 3 and 4, as resolution depends on the wireless controller firmware update scheduled under change CHG0030588. [Source: KB0009]

4. Link the incident ticket to problem record PRB0040021 to ensure proper tracking toward the permanent controller firmware fix. [Source: KB0009]

evidence:
State | Published

Version | 2

Category | network

Owner | Network Operations

Author | L. Haddad

Reviewed | 11 Apr 2026

Uses, 12 mo | 1,284 · Related PRB0040012, INC0010023

## Symptom.

The user can reach the internet but the VPN client reports an authentication failure. It began after a password reset. The client may report “invalid credentials” even when the new password is entered correctly.

## Cause.

The VPN client caches the previous credential in the operating system credential store. The cached entry is presented before the newly typed password, so the directory rejects it. Repeated attempts can lock the account (see KB0005).

## Resolution.

1. Confirm with the user that they changed their password within the last 24 hours.

2. Ask the user to sign out of the VPN client completely, including the system tray icon.

3. Clear the cached credential for the VPN profile from the credential store.

4. Reconnect using the new password.

5. If authentication still fails, check whether the account is locked in the identity console before escalating.

## Escalation.

If the account is not locked and the new password works elsewhere, escalate to the Network team with the client log.

## Symptom.

The connection drops every few minutes and reconnects on its own. It is worse in some parts of the building and while moving between areas.

## Cause.

Aggressive roaming behaviour between access points, or a power-saving setting on the wireless adapter that suspends the radio during idle periods.

## Resolution.

1. Establish whether drops occur in one location or while moving. Drops only while moving indicate roaming; drops while stationary indicate the adapter.

## Symptom.

The mail client displays Disconnected or Trying to connect. No new mail arrives. Webmail may still work, or may not.

## Cause.

Two distinct causes present identically: a single-user profile or cached-mode corruption, and a service-wide mail outage. Distinguishing them is the first step, not an afterthought.

## Resolution.

1. Ask whether colleagues are affected. If more than one user in the same area is affected, treat it as a service event and stop; do not apply per-user fixes to a platform outage.

2. Check whether webmail works for this user. If webmail works, the fault is client-side.

3. For a client-side fault, close the client fully and reopen it.

4. If it still fails, recreate the mail profile and allow the cache to rebuild.

5. Confirm mail flow before closing.

## Escalation.

If multiple users are affected, raise a major incident against the corporate-email service. Do not resolve individual incidents until the service event is closed.

## Symptom.

The order service returns HTTP 500 under load. Application logs report that the database connection pool is exhausted and that connection acquisition timed out.

## Cause.

Connections are held beyond their intended lifetime by a long-running query path and are not returned to the pool, so new requests wait and then fail.

## Resolution.

1. Do not restart the application server. A restart drops in-flight orders and caused a 40-minute outage on 14 March 2026.

2. Confirm pool saturation from the service metrics dashboard rather than from the error message alone.

3. Notify the Order Processing service owner. This service has a change-controlled remediation path.

4. Raise an emergency change against CHG0030455 for the pool drain procedure, which recycles connections without dropping in-flight work.

5. Apply the d

s without dropping in-flight work.

5. Apply the drain procedure only once the change is approved.

6. Monitor pool utilisation for thirty minutes after the drain.

## Escalation.

Any incident on order-processing at Priority 1 goes to the service owner immediately and is never remediated from the service desk alone.

State | Published

Version | 1

Service | sap-erp

Category | software

Owner | SAP Basis

Author | K. Selim

Reviewed | 06 Oct 2025

Uses, 12 mo | 203 · Related KE0000034, INC0010031

## Symptom.

The SAP GUI client fails to connect and reports RFC_ERROR_COMMUNICATION or a connection timeout. Other applications work normally.

## Cause.

The client cannot reach the message server on the required port. Most often the user is off the corporate network without the VPN, or the saved connection entry points at a decommissioned application server.

## Resolution.

1. Confirm the user is on the corporate network or connected to the VPN. SAP is not reachable from the internet.

2. Check the saved connection entry against the current published connection details.

3. If the entry names a specific application server, change it to the message server and group so that load balancing applies.

4. Reconnect and confirm sign-in reaches the logon screen.

5. If the timeout persists from a known-good network, check whether the message server is reach

network, check whether the message server is reachable on its port before escalating.

## Escalation.

A confirmed reachability failure from the corporate network goes to the SAP Basis team with the exact error text and the connection entry used.

## The trigger.

At 12:58 the order service began returning HTTP 500 under normal midday load. Connection pool saturation was reported in the application log within a minute, and monitoring raised INC0009884 at 13:02 as a P1.

## The response.

The analyst on the bridge searched the knowledge base, found KB0010, and applied it. Step 1 of that article, as it stood, instructed a restart of the application server.

## The consequence.

The restart cleared the pool as documented and simultaneously dropped every in-flight order. The service returned 200 within ninety seconds, so the restart looked successful on every signal the bridge was watching.

## The discovery.

Fulfilment noticed missing orders at 13:31. The bridge was reconvened, the gap was quantified at 47 unrecoverable orders, and manual recovery began.

## Restoration.

The service itself was never unavailable after 13:04. The forty minutes recorded above is the window in which orders were being accepted and lost, which is the number that matters commercially and the one this report uses.

The article was not wrong when it was written.

KB0010 v1 was published in 2023 against an earlier deployment where the service drained gracefully on shutdown. That behaviour changed with the 2025 platform migration and the article was never revisited.

## Symptom.

## Cause.

The local print spooler service has stalled, leaving orphaned job files that block the queue.

## Symptom.

The machine is noticeably slower after an update. Fans run constantly, applications are slow to launch, and the problem persists across restarts.

## Cause.

Post-update indexing and driver reinstallation run at high priority for a period after installation. If the degradation persists beyond that period, a driver mismatch is the usual cause.

3. If indexing dominates, allow it to complete and confirm with the user the following day.

4. If a graphics or storage driver dominates, reinstall the vendor driver for the installed operating system build.

5. Restart and confirm the machine returns to normal responsiveness

nfirm the machine returns to normal responsiveness.

If performance is still degraded 48 hours after the update with no dominant process, escalate to Endpoint Engineering with a performance capture.

## Symptom.

The user cannot sign in to any corporate system. Errors mention a locked or disabled account. Often follows a password change, and often presents as several services failing at once.

## Cause.

The lockout policy triggers after a threshold of failed attempts. A cached credential on any device – a phone mail profile, a VPN client, a mapped drive – can retry an old password silently and lock the account repeatedly, including immediately after each unlock.

## Resolution.

1. Verify the user's identity following the identity verification procedure. This step is mandatory and is never skipped.

2. Unlock the account in the identity console.

3. Ask the user to sign out of the corporate mail profile on their mobile device, which is the most common source of a silent retry.

4. Clear cached credentials on the laptop, including VPN and mapped drives.

5. Ask the user to sign in again and confirm access to two different services.

6. If the account lock

to two different services.

6. If the account locks again within minutes, a device is still retrying an old credential; identify it from the lockout source before unlocking a third time.

## Escalation.

Repeated lockouts with no identifiable source go to the Identity team. Never disable the lockout policy for an individual user.

## Cause.

The client cannot reach the message server on the required port. Most often the user is off the corporate network without the VPN, or the saved connection entry points at a decommissioned application server.

evidence:
State | Published

Version | 2

Service | corporate-wifi

Category | network

Owner | Network Operations

Author | L. Haddad

Reviewed | 02 Feb 2026

Uses, 12 mo | 1,041 · Related PRB0040021, INC0010033

## Symptom.

The connection drops every few minutes and reconnects on its own. It is worse in some parts of the building and while moving between areas.

## Cause.

Aggressive roaming behaviour between access points, or a power-saving setting on the wireless adapter that suspends the radio during idle periods.

## Resolution.

1. Establish whether drops occur in one location or while moving. Drops only while moving indicate roaming; drops while stationary indicate the adapter.

2. For a stationary user, disable power saving on the wireless adapter.

3. Update the wireless adapter driver to the current supported version.

4. Ask the user to forget and rejoin the corporate network so the profile is rebuilt.

5. Confirm a stable connection for at least fifteen minutes before closing.

## Escalation.

Drops affecting several users in the same area are an infrastructure fault. Escalate to Network with the location and the approximate times.

State | Published

Version | 2

Service | corporate-vpn

Category | network

Owner | Network Operations

Author | L. Haddad

Reviewed | 11 Apr 2026

Uses, 12 mo | 1,284 · Related PRB0040012, INC0010023

## Symptom.

The user can reach the internet but the VPN client reports an authentication failure. It began after a password reset. The client may report “invalid credentials” even when the new password is entered correctly.

## Cause.

The VPN client caches the previous credential in the operating system credential store. The cached entry is presented before the newly typed password, so the directory rejects it. Repeated attempts can lock the account (see KB0005).

## Resolution.

1. Confirm with the user that they changed their password within the last 24 hours.

2. Ask the user to sign out of the VPN client completely, including the system tray icon.

3. Clear the cached credential for the VPN profile from the credential store.

4. Reconnect using the new password.

5. If authentication still fails, check whether the account is locked in the identity console before escalating.

## Escalation.

If the account is not locked and the new password works elsewhere, escalate to the Network team with the client log.
